title: Fire Safety
disclaimer: General field guidance, not a legal document. Class letters, colours, distances and test intervals differ by country and by site fire-safety plan: check NFPA 10, EN 2/EN 3-7, IS 2190 and your local fire authority before relying on a figure marked verify.
fire_tetrahedron_note: Add the chemical chain reaction: removing any one element stops the fire.

classes.label: Class A — ordinary combustibles
classes.fuels: Wood, paper, cloth, cardboard, many plastics, rubber
examples: Pallets and packaging in a warehouse
classes.notes: Cooling is the main goal. Check for hidden smouldering after the flames are out.

classes.label: Class B — flammable liquids
classes.fuels: Petrol, diesel, solvents, paint, thinners, oils, alcohols
classes.notes: A straight water jet can spread burning liquid. Alcohol-type solvents need alcohol-resistant foam.

classes.label: Class C (EN 2) — flammable gases
classes.notes: Best action is to isolate the gas supply safely. Putting out a gas flame without stopping the leak can create an explosive atmosphere. In US NFPA 10 the letter C means energized electrical equipment instead.

classes.label: Class C (NFPA 10, USA) — energized electrical equipment
classes.notes: De-energize first if it is safe to do so; then treat as a Class A or B fire. In EN 2 there is no electrical class.

classes.label: Class D — combustible metals
classes.fuels: Magnesium, aluminium or titanium powder and swarf, sodium, lithium metal
classes.notes: Water and CO2 can make a metal fire worse. Use only the special dry powder made for the metal involved.

classes.label: Class F (EN 2) / Class K (NFPA 10) — cooking oils and fats
classes.notes: Never throw water on hot oil. Switch off the heat source if safe.

extinguishers.label: Water
extinguishers.notes: Cooling effect. Not on live electrical equipment or flammable liquids.

extinguishers.label: Water mist (de-ionised)
extinguishers.notes: Some water-mist types are rated for electrical equipment: follow the label, not assumption.

extinguishers.label: Foam (AFFF / AR-FFF)
extinguishers.notes: Alcohol-resistant foam for polar solvents. Not for live electrical equipment unless the label says so.

extinguishers.label: Carbon dioxide (CO2)
extinguishers.notes: No residue, good for electrical rooms. Asphyxiation risk in small or confined rooms: ventilate afterwards. Horn gets very cold: do not hold it.

extinguishers.label: Dry powder ABC (ammonium phosphate)
extinguishers.notes: General purpose. Reduces visibility and leaves corrosive residue on electronics and food areas. Clean up promptly.

extinguishers.label: Dry powder BC
extinguishers.notes: Fast knock-down of liquid and gas fires.

extinguishers.label: Dry powder for metal fires (Class D)
extinguishers.notes: Use only the powder approved for the specific metal. Apply gently to avoid scattering burning dust.

extinguishers.label: Wet chemical
extinguishers.notes: Forms a soapy layer on hot oil. Apply from a safe distance with a gentle sweep.

pass_steps.title: Pull
pass_steps.text: Pull the safety pin or break the tamper seal.

pass_steps.title: Aim
pass_steps.text: Aim the nozzle low at the base of the fire, not at the flames.

pass_steps.title: Squeeze
pass_steps.text: Squeeze the handle to discharge the agent.

pass_steps.title: Sweep
pass_steps.text: Sweep side to side across the base until the fire is out. Watch for re-ignition.

before_you_fight: Raise the alarm and call the emergency number first.
Fight a fire only if it is small, you are trained, you have a clear exit behind you and the right extinguisher is in your hand.
If the fire is bigger than a waste bin, or smoke is building, leave, close the door and go to the assembly point.
Never fight a fire involving gas cylinders under heat, unknown chemicals or a fire blocking your only exit.

notes: Mount where it is visible, accessible and along escape routes, with signage.
Do not block with stock or equipment. Keep the carrying handle at a height your site standard allows.
Maximum travel distance to an extinguisher depends on hazard class and local code (verify). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.157(d)(5) uses 75 ft (about 22.9 m) for Class A and 50 ft (about 15.25 m) for Class B.

inspection_checklist.item: Extinguisher is in its place, visible and not obstructed
Pressure gauge needle is in the green zone (or weight check done for CO2)
Safety pin in place and tamper seal unbroken
No dents, corrosion, leaks or damaged hose and nozzle
Operating instruction label is readable and faces outward
Correct extinguisher type for the hazard in that area
Service tag shows the annual maintenance by a competent person is in date
Pressure test (hydrostatic) is within the interval in the standard or manufacturer's instruction (verify)
Fire exits unlocked, clear and signs illuminated or visible
Fire alarm call points and panel show no fault
Fire doors close fully and are not wedged open
Assembly point is marked and reachable

fire_watch.title: Fire watch for hot work
fire_watch.purpose: Detect and stop any fire started by sparks, slag or heat during and after hot work.
fire_watch.duration_note: NFPA 51B and OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252 call for a fire watch during hot work and for at least 30 minutes afterwards. Your site permit or insurer may require longer (verify).
before_work: Hot work permit issued and signed; the area is checked by the issuer.
Combustibles within 11 m (35 ft) are removed or covered with fire-resistant blankets (verify local rule).
Floor and wall openings, drains and cracks are covered so sparks cannot travel.
Correct extinguisher at hand and the fire watcher knows how to use it.
Gas test done if flammable vapour could be present.
fire_watcher_duties: Watch the area, including the other side of walls and floors below, for sparks and smoke.
Stay until the end of the watch period; no other duties.
Know the alarm and emergency numbers; stop the work if conditions change.
Sign off the permit when the watch is complete.

drills.frequency_note: At least twice a year is common practice; the legal minimum depends on the country and occupancy (verify).

roles.duty: Sweeps the assigned area, closes doors and sends everyone to the assembly point.
Takes the headcount at the assembly point against the attendance list.
Triggers the alarm and calls the fire service / emergency number.
Waits at the assembly point with the first-aid kit.

steps: Announce the drill to management only; workers should react as to a real alarm.
Sound the alarm, start the stopwatch and note the time to clear the building.
Check every exit route is used, and no one uses the lift.
Do a headcount at the assembly point and list anyone missing.
Debrief the same day: what was slow, what was blocked, who did not hear the alarm.
Record the drill (date, time, evacuation time, issues, corrective actions with owners and dates).

NFPA 51B Standard for Fire Prevention During Welding, Cutting and Other Hot Work
